title: The four object types, opened up
summary: Blob, tree, commit and tag are the entire data model. Read each one in its raw form, compute a sha by hand, and see why identical content is stored exactly once.
mental_model: Git stores four kinds of object, each named by the sha-1 of its type, length and content. A commit points to a tree, a tree points to blobs and other trees, and a tag points to any of them. That is the entire database.

steps.title: Count what one commit created
steps.why: Four files, but not four objects — plus trees for each directory and one commit. `cat-file --batch-all-objects` lists everything in the database with its type.
steps.expect: Blobs, trees, a commit and a tag — and fewer blobs than you might expect.

steps.title: Two identical files, one blob
steps.why: pump.py and dosing.py have identical content, so they hash to the same sha and are stored once. Git deduplicates by content automatically — this is why moving a file costs nothing.
steps.expect: The same sha twice, in two index rows with different paths.

verify.cmd: sh -c 'test "$(git hash-object src/pump.py)" = "$(git hash-object src/dosing.py)" && echo identical'
verify.label: identical content shares one blob

steps.title: Read a blob
steps.why: A blob is content and nothing else — no filename, no permissions, no timestamp. Everything about where it lives is recorded in the tree that references it.
steps.expect: blob, its size in bytes, then the file content.

steps.title: Read the tree
steps.why: A tree is a directory listing: mode, type, sha, name. Note `src` is a tree of its own — directories nest, and this recursion is the whole structure.
steps.expect: The root tree with two subtrees, and src listing both python files pointing at the SAME blob sha.

steps.title: Read the commit
steps.why: A commit is a short text object: the tree it snapshots, its parents, author, committer, and the message. Nothing else. The 'diff' you see in `git show` is computed on demand, never stored.
steps.expect: tree, author, committer and message lines — and no parent, since this is the first commit.

steps.title: Read the tag object
steps.why: An annotated tag is the fourth type: it points at an object, names its type, and carries a tagger and a message. A lightweight tag has no object at all — it is just a ref file.
steps.expect: The tag object's sha differs from the commit's; `^{}` dereferences to the commit.

verify.label: the annotated tag is its own object

verify.cmd: sh -c 'test "$(git rev-parse v1.0)" != "$(git rev-parse v1.0^{})" && echo different'
verify.label: the tag object and the commit it points at have different shas

steps.title: Compute a sha yourself
steps.why: The hash covers the type, a space, the length, a NUL byte, then the content. Reproducing it with a shell one-liner proves there is no hidden metadata — the name really is a function of the content.
steps.expect: The same forty characters from both.

steps.title: Watch a change ripple upwards
steps.why: Editing one file changes its blob, which changes its tree, which changes the root tree, which changes the commit. Every sha on the path to the root is different — that chain is what makes history tamper-evident.
commands: sh -c 'echo docs subtree unchanged: $(git rev-parse HEAD~1^{tree}:docs) $(git rev-parse HEAD^{tree}:docs)'
steps.expect: New root tree and new src tree — but the docs subtree keeps its original sha, because nothing in it changed.

verify.cmd: sh -c 'test "$(git rev-parse HEAD~1^{tree}:docs)" = "$(git rev-parse HEAD^{tree}:docs)" && echo shared'
verify.label: unchanged directories are reused, not copied
verify.hint: that is why a commit is cheap even in a huge repository

verify.label: you identified all four object types

verify.cmd: sh -c 'test "$(git rev-parse HEAD~1^{tree}:docs)" = "$(git rev-parse HEAD^{tree}:docs)" && echo shared'
verify.label: unchanged subtrees are shared between commits

verify.cmd: sh -c 'test "$(git rev-parse HEAD~1^{tree})" != "$(git rev-parse HEAD^{tree})" && echo changed'
verify.label: …while the path from the change to the root is all new objects
two commits, both readable as raw objects

pitfalls: Blobs have no filename. A file 'moved' between commits is the same blob referenced from a different tree — which is why rename detection is a diff-time heuristic.
`HEAD^{tree}` dereferences a commit to its tree; `v1.0^{}` dereferences a tag to its commit. The braces matter, and some shells need them quoted.
Git stores whole snapshots, not diffs. Delta compression happens later, inside packfiles, and is an optimisation rather than the data model.
Modern git can use sha-256 instead of sha-1, but the structure is identical — only the hash function changes.
cheatsheet: the commit a tag points at
